query: In conventional alloys, loss of toughness has long been associated with grain-boundary segregation and brittle grain-boundary precipitation. By contrast, compositionally complex high-entropy alloys can suppress rapid grain coarsening and deleterious intermetallic formation and have shown favorable strength–ductility combinations and resistance to high-temperature softening and low-temperature embrittlement. These findings do not establish what governs possible toughness degradation in an initially single-phase high-entropy alloy. Under the constraint of retaining a compositionally complex alloy suitable for demanding engineering service, what testable mechanistic hypothesis explains whether and why brittle behavior emerges? Specify a controlled comparison that would distinguish the hypothesis from conventional-alloy expectations, predicted observations relative to the initial baseline, its service and loading boundaries, supporting prior evidence, and a decisive falsification outcome.

generation.hypothesis: Under cyclic mechanical loading at intermediate temperatures, a single‐phase high-entropy alloy experiences stress‐induced localized nanoscale compositional fluctuations that trigger the formation of intragranular, chemically ordered regions. These regions act as brittle microstructural precipitates that concentrate strain and nucleate cracks, leading to brittle behavior despite the alloy’s overall homogeneous disordered state.
generation.material_initial_state: A single-phase, compositionally complex high-entropy alloy with a homogeneous, disordered solid-solution microstructure.
generation.intervention: Apply controlled cyclic mechanical loading at intermediate temperatures (e.g., 300–500°C) to provoke stress-assisted atomic diffusion.
generation.conditions: Testing under cyclic loading conditions representative of service conditions, with a comparison control sample subjected to monotonic (constant) loading under the same temperature regime.
generation.structural_mediator: Nanoscale, intragranular chemically ordered regions (transient microprecipitates) formed by local segregation of minor alloying elements.
generation.mechanism: During cyclic loading, mechanical strain promotes short-range atomic diffusion that overcomes local energy barriers, leading to the clustering of certain elements into ordered arrangements within grains. These clusters reduce local toughness by serving as stress concentrators and initiating microcracks, differing from conventional alloys where brittle behavior is linked primarily to grain-boundary segregation or intergranular precipitates.
generation.predicted_outcome: Under cyclic loading, microstructural characterization (via TEM or atom probe tomography) will reveal nanoscale ordered regions within grains, and fracture analysis will show crack initiation at these sites. In contrast, specimens under monotonic loading will lack such ordered regions and maintain ductile behavior.
generation.baseline: The alloy’s initial homogeneous, disordered single-phase state with high ductility, as observed under monotonic loading at comparable temperatures.
generation.boundary: The effect is expected to manifest under cyclic loading conditions at temperatures around 300–500°C and stress amplitudes near the alloy’s yield strength. Outside of this regime (e.g., under purely monotonic loading or at temperatures far outside this range), the formation of ordered regions and resultant brittle behavior are not anticipated.
generation.uncertainty: The exact kinetics of nanoscale segregation and ordering under cyclic loading, including the minimum strain amplitude and number of cycles required, remain uncertain.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare identical samples of the high-entropy alloy and subject one set to cyclic loading at 300–500°C while maintaining another set under monotonic loading at the same temperature. Use in-situ TEM and atom probe tomography to monitor any nanoscale compositional ordering during and after loading. Also, conduct fracture toughness tests to correlate microstructural changes with mechanical properties.
measurements: In-situ TEM imaging to detect nanoscale ordered regions
Atom probe tomography for mapping local compositional fluctuations
Fracture toughness and crack initiation site analysis
Comparative analysis between cyclically and monotonically loaded samples
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If cyclically loaded samples do not display the formation of nanoscale, intragranular ordered regions, or if brittle fracture occurs through mechanisms similar to conventional grain-boundary precipitation rather than through intragranular features, then the hypothesis is falsified.

frame.system: A compositionally complex, initially single‐phase high-entropy alloy (HEA) that is engineered to avoid deleterious intermetallic formation and rapid grain coarsening under service conditions.
frame.goal: To establish a testable mechanistic hypothesis that explains the onset of brittle behavior (toughness degradation) in high-entropy alloys, distinguishing its origin from that in conventional alloys.
frame.limitation: Despite favorable strength–ductility and resistance to softening/embrittlement in many conditions, it is not known what internal mechanism triggers the transition from ductile to brittle behavior in these single-phase HEAs.
constraints: the alloy must remain compositionally complex and applicable for demanding engineering service
the hypothesis must account for the suppression of traditional grain-boundary deleterious phenomena observed in conventional alloys
frame.regime: Service and loading conditions spanning high-temperature softening, low-temperature embrittlement, and relevant mechanical stress tests (e.g., tensile, fracture toughness tests) under controlled environments that simulate real-world engineering applications.
prior_attempts: Conventional models have primarily correlated brittleness with grain-boundary segregation and precipitation in simpler alloy systems, but these are insufficiently explanatory for HEAs where such processes are suppressed.
Past approaches assumed similar mechanisms in HEAs without controlled comparisons to reveal unique HEA-specific behaviors.

families.best_lever: Implement an accelerated aging protocol (or controlled stress test) on one HEA sample to induce local ordering or nanoscale fluctuations and compare its fracture toughness and crack-tip plasticity with a baseline sample under identical loading conditions.

families.principle: Using advanced, in-situ characterization techniques to directly observe nanoscale compositional fluctuations and local ordering dynamics during service-relevant conditions.
cues_for: post-mortem analyses to identify local transformations

families.best_lever: Utilize in-situ high-resolution TEM or atom probe tomography during controlled mechanical/thermal loading to capture the emerging nanoscale ordering or clustering that might herald a ductile-to-brittle transition.

decision.trend: Early studies in high-entropy alloys sought parallels with conventional alloys by attributing toughness loss to grain-boundary phenomena like segregation and precipitation. However, PMC6897545 revealed that in a single-phase CrMnFeCoNi alloy, nanoclustering of specific elements (Cr, Ni, Mn) at the grain boundaries leads to decohesion even when traditional intermetallic precipitation is suppressed. Later, work such as PMC9848264 demonstrated that modifying grain-boundary morphology via controlled heat treatments (yielding serrated rather than straight boundaries) can mitigate hot ductility drop by dispersing strain concentrations. Overall, researchers have moved from assuming conventional segregation processes to identifying subtle nano‐structural and microchemical changes at grain boundaries as critical to toughness degradation in compositionally complex alloys.
decision.unsolved: While these studies indicate that grain-boundary nanoclustering and morphology modifications influence brittle behavior, the precise mechanistic pathway for the emergence of brittleness in an initially single‐phase high-entropy alloy remains unresolved. It is still unclear how controlled changes in the grain-boundary state, in the absence of classical intermetallic formation, govern the transition from ductile to brittle fracture under service and loading conditions.
decision.lever: Systematically vary heat-treatment parameters (such as cooling rate) to engineer controlled differences in grain-boundary nanoclustering and morphology (e.g., from straight to serrated boundaries) while keeping overall phase stability and composition constant, and then compare mechanical responses (tensile, fracture toughness tests) under service-relevant conditions.
decision.why: This experiment directly tests the hypothesis that brittle behavior in high-entropy alloys originates from HEA-specific grain-boundary phenomena (namely, the evolution of nanoclusters that reduce boundary cohesion) rather than conventional segregation-induced precipitation. The controlled comparison of samples with and without engineered grain-boundary modifications provides a decisive means to distinguish the mechanism, following the trend established by earlier studies.
